newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Loose money policy seen on low Taiwan inflation.
newsitem.headline: Loose money policy seen on low Taiwan inflation.

text.p: Taiwan's low inflation in March has given the central bank ample leeway to keep money supply loose, although the recent big rally on the stock market makes new measures unlikely, analysts said on Monday.
The March consumer price index rose 1.09 percent compared to March 1996, well below analysts' expectations, the Directorate General of Budget, Accounting and Statistics said on Monday.
An April 3 Reuters Poll of Taiwan economists had forecast an average CPI growth of 2.55 percent.
"(The low growth) gives the central bank ample excuse to maintain its stable-to-loose monetary policy to boost the still slowly recovering economy," said HSBC James Capel economist Stephen Wang.
"But I quite doubt the accuracy of the inflation figure. Such a surprisingly low figure fits too well into the government's intention to keep liquidity loose to boost the economy," Wang said.

The directorate gave three reasons for the low March CPI figure: a decline in service charges after the mid-February Chinese Lunar New Year holiday, abundant supplies of vegetables and fruits, and a decline in pork prices in late March due to an outbreak of hog foot and mouth disease.
Various government agencies have estimated that the hog epidemic, reported on March 20, would reduce the island's 1997 gross domestic product growth by 0.39-0.50 percentage points.
Thus, the government's forecast for 1997 GDP growth of 6.28 percent would likely be cut to 5.78-5.89 percent.

Analysts said the low inflation in March may be a hint that the central bank would loosen banks' reserve requirements to boost the economy -- a move the central bank has said it would make at an "appropriate time".

"In theory, the central bank might think the time is appropriate for it to lower reserve requirements to boost the economy hit by the hog disease," said Grand Cathay Securities vice-president Terry Chen.
"But I believe it's unlikely for the central bank to do so at a time when the stock market has rallied so much," Chen said.
On Monday, the stock index surged 150.13 points, or 1.79 percent, to 8,517.70, closing higher for the fourth straight session. The index has risen 23 percent so far in 1997.
The central bank recently said it would keep its "stable-to-loose, but not-too-loose" money policy, a somewhat cautious approach aimed at cooling the stock market.

Analysts said they expected Taiwan's inflation to stay at low levels in the first half of 1997, but it should encounter pressure to rise in the second half because oil and utilities prices were likely to rise.
"Likely rises in utilities and oil prices in the second half and possible typhoon damages will give pressure on the CPI to rise," said Nomura Securities economist Amy Huang.
Taiwan's annual typhoon season is from June to October.
State monopoly Chinese Petroleum Corp raised oil prices by an average 2.97 percent on Saturday. The directorate said on Monday the hike would add 0.13 percentage points to the consumer price index.
But analysts said Taiwan's 1997 CPI growth still should fall within the 3.0 percent growth target set by the cabinet's Council for Economic Planning and Development.
In the first three months of 1997, the CPI grew an average 1.70 percent over the same period last year.
